prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for the new account of exporting, foreign investment and the gains from trade that followed

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity with selection into exporting (Melitz 2003; Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple 2004) changed the questions trade economics asks. Trade is analysed through reallocation across firms and not through representative firms or sectors. The framework added a productivity-selection channel to the gains from trade and gave the exports-versus-FDI sorting result. It is also a workhorse well outside trade, in macro, growth and productivity analysis, which matters to me as a macroeconomist who uses such models. The core papers are more than twenty years old, so there has been ample time to test them against firm-level data and to extend them structurally. All eleven openings rank the entry first or second, and I treat that only as a sign of broad scientific agreement. The credit is also fairly compact. Melitz supplies the canonical selection model, and Helpman combines the HMY extension with a longer record in trade theory. A two-person prize therefore matches the discovery without stretching it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related and in part parallel contributions, on exporter premia and on the Eaton-Kortum framework, and they are outside the credited names. Redding is credited here and would be omitted. The baseline Melitz model is also rejected in some details, for example in its distributional and welfare implications, and the quantitative-trade lineage (B037) is arguably where much of the applied weight now sits. A committee could reasonably decide that the discovery is a family of contributions and not a clean pair. Helpman's overlap with B047 also leaves open how his work should be packaged.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the BLP and dynamic-oligopoly entry (B006) first on methodological and applied impact beyond industrial organisation, with a clean BLP core, and puts B001 second.
responses.response: I agree that B006 is a very strong candidate. It is mature, the BLP attribution is cleaner than in most entries, and it is a rare case of a tool that changed practice in antitrust and policy. I still rank B001 above it, for two reasons. First, B001 changed what the field theorises as well as how it estimates. Second, the Melitz framework is used well beyond its home field. I accept that this is a judgement and not a decisive scientific argument, and B006 stays on my alternatives list. I would like the committee to look hard at whether the Pakes dynamic-games strand and the BLP demand strand form one discovery or two, since that decides whether the three-name set Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes is the right boundary.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first but flags that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important parallel contributors outside the credited set, and notes that Krugman's earlier prize covered part of the new-trade-theory lineage.
responses.response: I agree that the missing parallel contributors are the main attribution risk, and I would not wave it away. I think it is manageable. Bernard and Jensen's facts on exporter premia motivated and tested the theory, but the formal selection mechanism and its extension to exports versus FDI are Melitz's and Helpman's. Krugman's prize recognised trade under increasing returns and product differentiation with representative firms. Firm-level selection is a separate step, so I do not see duplication. I would still like the committee to check how much weight the empirical-facts lineage deserves in a citation. I have made the citation about theory and its consequences for that reason.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B006 first, and cites the field's recent prize history (trade not honoured since 2008, industrial organisation not since 2014) as part of the timing case, while still putting B001 second.
responses.response: I would not rely on field rotation as an argument. It says nothing about which discovery is more fundamental, and it cuts both ways, since either field could be called overdue. I agree with your scientific point that both candidates are mature and have wide influence outside their home fields. Where I differ is on breadth of conceptual change, which I think favours B001. I also think your concern about where to draw the boundary of the discovery applies to B006 more than to B001.

responses.point: Andersson proposes Helpman and Melitz and leaves out Redding because his quantitative and spatial work is a later extension and less central to this discovery, while asking whether a three-person split might be preferred.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person core and with the reasoning. Redding's contribution is substantial, but it belongs mostly to the quantitative and spatial strand (B037) and not to the selection mechanism. Adding him would shift the citation toward a different discovery, and I would want a separate case for that. A third name added only to fill the slots would weaken the attribution.

uncertainties: How the committee should weigh the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributions, which are outside the credited names, against a two-person prize on the theory of selection.
Whether the discovery is best framed as firm heterogeneity and selection (B001) or as the broader quantitative-trade tradition (B037), and whether Redding's claim is stronger than I judge it.
Whether B006 should be preferred on cleaner attribution and demonstrated applied reach, given that the choice depends partly on how much weight theory and methods receive.
How to package Helpman's work given his appearance in B047.
My assessments rely on general knowledge from the supplied openings and profile. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or award history.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the B001 credited names (Helpman, Melitz, Redding) is apparent from my supplied profile. The profile does list professional ties to colleagues in this committee. Timo Boppart, a co-opted member, is a repeat co-author, including on the 2018 Myrdal Prize article, and John Hassler, the chair, is a long-term co-author. Neither is a candidate in B001. Several long-term co-authors, such as Giovanni Violante and Aleh Tsyvinski, work in macro and are not credited in B001. I disclose these and do not adjudicate them.
